newsitem.title: JAPAN: Espresso makers hope to ride Japan's 'Italia boom'.
newsitem.headline: Espresso makers hope to ride Japan's 'Italia boom'.

text.p: They've shown a penchant for pizza and a soft spot for spaghetti, and soon more Japanese diners will be raising their cups for another Italian specialty -- espresso coffee.
At least that is the hope of Japan's coffee roasters and retailers.

But despite a slew of recent tie-ups with Italian roasters, industry officials say it is still too early to tell if espresso will filter into everyday Japanese life, as it has in the United States, or quickly fade away as a passing fancy.
"We see significant growth potential for espresso coffee in Japan," said Masahiro Ito of the publicity section at Kataoka Co Ltd, a leading Japanese importer of coffees and teas.
"In line with the growing popularity of Italian food and a recent rise in European-style cafes here, the number of people who enjoy espresso coffee has been increasing," he said.
Japan is the world's third-largest coffee consumer after the United States and Germany.

Kataoka signed a sales pact in January with Italy's largest coffee producer, Luigi Lavazza Spa, and started distributing its espresso beans and powder to Japanese retailers and restaurants in February.
The company aims to boost sales of espresso coffee to around six billion yen ($48.7 million) within the next few years.

Suntory Ltd, a leading Japanese maker of distilled spirits and beverages, has also joined hands with an Italian espresso maker, Illycaffe Spa, and began selling its brand of espresso coffee beans last November.
Suntory began importing Italian foods in 1988 and sales have grown sharply as Japanese show an increasing interest in Italian culture and cuisine, a company spokesman said.

"There is an espresso boom around the world. In the U.S., the market share of espresso coffee is now about 35 percent, compared with about five percent 10 years ago," the spokesman said. "In Japan as well, signs are emerging that espresso coffee consumption will grow," he said.
Other Japanese coffee producers say they see the same signs.
Key Coffee Inc, Japan's leading producer of regular coffee, launched a new espresso coffee product last autumn.

"The espresso coffee traditionally sold in Japan was different from that in Milan, more bitter and lower in quality. We hope that genuine espresso coffee will take hold in the Japanese market," a spokesman for Key Coffee said.

Japan's coffee consumption for regular coffee and instant coffee in calendar 1996 was estimated at around 470 billion yen ($3.82 billion), against 468 billion yen ($3.80 billion) in 1995, according to the All Japan Coffee Association.

Espresso's share is still minuscule in the Japanese coffee market, long dominated by the strong European blend favoured by Japanese coffee drinkers and the weaker American variation. There are still few cafes or restaurants aside from specialty shops offering espresso in Japan.
"There are hurdles ahead (that must be overcome) if espresso is to become a part of daily life in Japan and not just a fad," said an official at the All Japan Coffee Association.
"The key is whether Japanese will take a liking to it and whether the costs of roasting equipment can be brought down," he said.
